items.title: Jane Austen’s daily piano warm-up may hold a surprisingly simple lesson about creativity
items.summary:
Jane Austen published four novels during her lifetime, with two more appearing after her death. Then there are the numerous poems , plays, and parodies she wrote in her youth, along with the lengthy letters she continued writing throughout her life. Even more impressive than the output, however, is the lasting influence of Austen’s work.

For many writers, that kind of creative consistency comes with a routine. Writers throughout history have developed their own rituals for getting into the right headspace to work, whether that means writing at the same time every day, working in a particular place, or starting the day with an activity that has nothing to do with writing.

Austen had her own version of a creative warm-up: before settling in to write, she would sit down at the pianoforte.

Jane Austen started her creative day with music 

During her years at Chawton Cottage, which happened to be one of the most productive periods of her career, Austen played the pianoforte every morning before serving her family breakfast. According to her niece Caroline Austen , “Aunt Jane began her day with music.”

Austen’s family owned around 600 pieces of music, including works by Mozart, Haydn, and Clementi, so she had plenty to choose from. Music also found its way into her novels, where several characters play the piano, and scholars have noted the musicality imbued into Austen’s prose.

Her morning practice also ran against some of the expectations around women and music at the time. The Jane Austen Society of North America notes that piano playing could be viewed as a “frivolous”…
items.t: Jane Austen’s daily piano warm-up may hold a surprisingly simple lesson about creativity

items.title: Sea urchins have a bizarre habit of wearing shells as hats. A fun video shows why they do it.
items.summary:
There are plenty of animals with impressive survival strategies, but sea urchins may have one of the most entertaining ones. Some of them have taken their already unusual appearance a step further by developing a habit that makes them look like they’re wearing tiny hats . Adaptation at its most adorable? We think so. 

A fun video from BBC Earth shows these creatures picking up shells and other bits of debris and placing them on top of their bodies as they strut across the ocean floor. 

Sea urchins use thousands of tiny tube feet to move around and interact with objects in their environment. Those same appendages allow them to grab pieces of material from the seafloor and position them over their bodies, creating what looks like a miniature collection of ocean-floor accessories.

Aside from providing a delightful dose of underwater whimsy, this behavior has a very practical purpose.

More than a bold fashion choice 

Researchers have been studying this phenomenon for decades, and one major reason sea urchins cover themselves is to protect against UV light. That can be especially important in shallow water, where sunlight is stronger. It may also become more useful as kelp forests decline, since the towering plants often act as a natural canopy for sea urchins and countless other marine animals.

There is a complication here, though. Sea urchins eat kelp, and when their populations grow too large, they can contribute to the loss of entire kelp forests. So the animals can help shape the very habitat that provides them with protection. When that canopy disappears, an urchin…
items.t: Sea urchins have a bizarre habit of wearing shells as hats. A fun video shows why they do it.

items.summary:
Actor Charlie Chaplin and actress Sophia Loren developed a strong relationship Chaplin, whose career began in silent film in 1914 , was someone Loren looked up to.

So when the legendary actor asked the Italian actress to be in the 1967 film he was directing, A Countess from Hong Kong , she was thrilled. 

“When Charlie Chaplin asked me to do ( A Countess from Hong Kong , 1967) I was really very, very happy. I would never have thought that he was going to ask me to be the lead in his last film. It was a wonderful relationship between me and Charlie Chaplin,” she told the South China Morning Post .

Loren shared in her 2014 memoir Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow: My Life that Chaplin had come into her life in the 1960s. And it was during this time together that Chaplin pointed out a major flaw he saw in Loren. He subsequently offered her advice at 50-years-old that had a profound impact and changed her life.

View this post on Instagram 

Loren and Chaplin’s friendship blossoms 

Loren recalled her excitement to work with the Hollywood legend.

“I was so nervous working with him. He’s such a master. But on the first day on the set, I realized he was just as nervous. If you care and love something, you get nervous. I’m suspicious of people who don’t ever get nervous,” she told The Wrap .

She also told The Los Angeles Times , “[Writer-director] Charlie Chaplin wanted me because he saw a picture I did with [Vittorio] De Sica, maybe it was ‘Gold of Naples,’ and he said ‘I want this girl.’ He could have given me the telephone book and I would have done it anyway.”

items.title: Social psychologist found a simple conversation habit that instantly makes people more likable
items.summary:
When you’re hanging out in a low-stakes social situation, like a lazy Sunday barbecue or gabbing with your neighbor while he waters his lawn, it’s easy to fall into the trap of being vague. How often do you hear these types of responses to simple small-talk questions?

“How’s it going?”

“It’s going.”

“What did you do last weekend?”

“Nothing, just hung out.”

“Did you see the game last night?”

“Yeah, total bummer.”

Vague answers make you less likable 

A 2024 study from James Cook University in Singapore, by Dr. Deming (Adam) Wang and his team, found that when people give vague answers, others see them as less likable than those who give full details. The study also found that people are less likely to want to date or befriend someone who gives ambiguous answers. 

Two people chatting over champagne. Credit: Canva 

When people give vague answers, even in low-stakes social situations, people think they are trying to conceal something or aren’t interested in interacting with them. Vague people are also judged as being less warm, less extraverted, less gullible, and more cautious.

“When asked a question, people often give responses that are not as precise as the questioner had hoped for. Sometimes this vagueness is deliberate, but other times the responder could just be tired, distracted, or genuinely unable to recall the specific answer to a question,” Wang remarked . “Our research reveals the impact of vague responses on likeability. It emphasises the importance of clear communication in daily life, because likeability pulls some serious weight in both our social and…
items.t: Social psychologist found a simple conversation habit that instantly makes people more likable

items.title: Woman’s knowledge of fashion history cracked a 120-year-old Fabergé mystery after a museum visit
items.summary:
In 2019, Geoffrey Munn, the jewelry expert from “ Antiques Roadshow ,” was looking through the storerooms of the Brighton Museum & Art Gallery in England when he noticed the corner of a frame poking out of some archival tissue paper.

It turned out to be one of five forgotten Fabergé pieces, including two gold-mounted picture frames, each holding a photograph of an elegant woman in furs, lace and pearls. Nobody knew who the women were. Munn and two of the museum’s curators had tried to find out but came up empty.

So when the Fabergé pieces went on display in 2021, the museum added a sign asking visitors for help.

View this post on Instagram 

In March 2024, actor and screenwriter Andreane Rellou ( @andreanerellou ), who’s from Athens and based in London, visited the museum with her sister and read it. Then she went home and started digging.

“I used my knowledge of historical fashion and hairstyling to try and date the pictures myself,” Rellou told the museum . She guessed the woman in the smaller, square frame was in her early 40s, and her clothes and hair pointed to the early 1900s. And because Fabergé frames have always been expensive, she figured the woman had serious money.

View this post on Instagram 

That meant she had likely married in the 1880s, and she had married well.

“At that point, I searched through debutante portraits, and then I looked through lists of recently married men of the upper classes … and the Rothschild name came up,” Rellou told Smithsonian .

“I gasped when I came across Marie Perugia’s portrait from the Rothschild Archive website,” she…
items.t: Woman’s knowledge of fashion history cracked a 120-year-old Fabergé mystery after a museum visit

items.title: There aren’t enough adjectives to describe how mind-blowing the making of ‘Wildwood’ actually was
items.summary:
If you have the chance to see Wildwood on the big screen , definitely do it. But I highly recommend diving into the making of the film before you go, instead of after. 

I promise, you won’t ruin any of the movie magic by peeking behind the curtain first. In fact, you can’t fully appreciate how magical it truly is unless you get a glimpse of why it took 16 years to plan and create it.

Wildwood is like no animated film you’ve ever seen 

If you’ve seen Laika Studios’ other films (such as Coraline , ParaNorman , Kubo and the Two Strings ) and understand how they were made, you might be able to appreciate Wildwood for what it is. But even at that, Laika has never done a stop-motion film on the scale of Wildwood , and neither has anyone else. 

When I say there aren’t enough adjectives to describe how mind-blowing it is, I’m being literal. It’s not that the story itself is outstanding; it’s based on a fantasy book series and has the elements you’d expect. But the artistry that went into telling that story and the layers of human creativity beneath it deserve all the accolades, because WOW . 

16,000 handmade feathers for just one character 

Laika Studios creates elaborate handmade sets for all of its films, paying attention to the tiniest of details. And in Wildwood , there are a lot—like a lot —of details. 

For intance, a golden eagle named The General, who helps the main character, Prue, was created with 16,000 individual, handmade feathers across several different puppets. And that was just one bird. This film is full of birds, in addition to humans, coyotes, and more.…
items.t: There aren’t enough adjectives to describe how mind-blowing the making of ‘Wildwood’ actually was

items.title: The man who wrote the Carpenters’ bank jingle also gave a frog his signature song
items.summary:
Musician and composer Paul Williams was very busy in the 1970s . He was not only writing brilliant hit songs, but truly famous people were taking note. The likes of David Bowie, the Carpenters, Three Dog Night, Helen Reddy and even Jim Henson (of the Muppets fame) helped get him many well-deserved accolades.

In a podcast interview with Smashing Pumpkins lead singer Billy Corgan, Williams explains how his career esculated. “Roger (Nichols) and I were writing all these songs. And we had met the Carpenters . Incidentally, Roger and I were getting all these cuts. And nothing was ever on the radio. I mean, album cuts, B-sides. Nothing on there. I mean, nobody knew who we were. There was no real chart success, but we were making a great living. B-sides! I mean, I wrote the B-sides of ‘I Am Woman’ and ‘Delta Dawn.’”

Meet the Carpenters 

He continues, “So all of a sudden, there’s a knock at the door in Roger’s office, and it’s Chuck Kaye and Herb Alpert and they said, ‘This is our newest act at A&M (records). Wanted you to meet Karen and Richard Carpenter.’ And they looked at Roger and I were like, ‘Oh man, we love your Peppermint Trolley cut of ‘Trust’ and the Steve Lawrence recording of ‘Drifter.’ And we’re like, ‘We’re famous, oh my God.’ We’re so excited because these two kids knew who we were.

Williams shares how exciting things got. “When they recorded ‘Close to You,’ which was their first huge hit, the B-side was ‘I Kept on Loving You,’ that Roger and I wrote. It was going to be the A-side, but they turned it over and played ‘Close to You’ because was a major, major…
items.t: The man who wrote the Carpenters’ bank jingle also gave a frog his signature song

items.title: Robert De Niro’s CIA buddy shared an ‘uncomfortable’ part of his training. The actor turned it into the scene that made ‘Meet the Parents.’
items.summary:
Some movie moments are so quintessentially perfect , they’re destined to become a classic from the opening frame . The lie detector scene in Meet the Parents is one of them. Except it almost never existed at all.

With Focker-In-Law arriving soon , the cringe-and-comedy franchise is returning to theaters. But the signature scene that had us all shaking with laughter more than 25 years ago wasn’t in the original screenplay.

You know the moment. Robert De Niro plays Jack Byrnes, a suspicious dad who happens to be ex-CIA. When he catches his daughter’s fiancé snooping around his basement, he hooks him up to a polygraph machine. Then starts asking questions that Ben Stiller’s Greg Focker has no idea how to answer. Greg’s anxious sweating and fidgeting comically causes the polygraph needle to jump all over the place, leaving his future father-in-law to wonder: is Greg a truthful man worthy of marrying his daughter? Does he deserve to be in his family’s “circle of trust”? The scene is a perfect blend of high discomfort and big laughs, but where did it come from?

A friend, a confession, and a bad day at work 

De Niro had already met some real-life CIA contacts while doing research for a future role. They shared personal stories with him about their agency training days. One element stood out to the actor as particularly intriguing: the polygraph test. De Niro says his CIA buddies described the process as deeply uncomfortable, invasive, and tense. It was the kind of experience he felt would stay with a person long after the questions stop.

The conversation stuck with De Niro,…
items.t: Robert De Niro’s CIA buddy shared an ‘uncomfortable’ part of his training. The actor turned it into the scene that made ‘Meet the Parents.’

items.title: A Monkee wanted to show people his new song. The film he made pointed toward the future of MTV.
items.summary:
Alt Subhed: Mike Nesmith was told no one would watch music on TV. He proved them wrong.

Alt Subhed: Music fans never saw Mike Nesmith’s second act coming, let alone his third.

Between the British Invasion and the birth of Flower Power, pop music was constantly transforming during the Swinging Sixties. From Detroit’s Motown empire to the folk-rock evolution, new sounds could pop up anywhere. Even television . 

In the late 1960s, Michael Nesmith became a household name . He was the sarcastic, wool-hat-wearing member of The Monkees . Together with his bandmates, he starred in the band’s popular NBC television sitcom of the same name. For many artists, being in the “Prefab Four” might be the absolute peak of their career. But for Nesmith, being a Monkee was just the first chapter of a much larger story.

Beneath Nesmith’s laconic, twang-infused persona lived a relentless visionary. Turns out it runs in the family. In his autobiography, Infinite Tuesdays , he attributed his inquisitive mind to his mother. Bette Nesmith Graham, you see, invented Liquid Paper . And while Michael grew up comfortable, he yearned more than anything to make music. 

NBC cancelled The Monkees sitcom after 58 episodes, but Nesmith’s artistic journey was just beginning. He co-wrote the script for The Monkees cult-classic film, “Head.” His collaborator on the story was none other than actor Jack Nicholson . And after the band’s breakup, Nesmith started a journey that fundamentally changed how people consume music and media. 

The accidental birth of the modern music video

items.title: Thomas Jefferson coined a hip and funny phrase for abrupt goodbyes that still holds up today
items.summary:
“Irish goodbye” is a term for when someone slips out of an event without telling anyone, avoiding the awkwardness of announcing their departure. (Though the Irish didn’t necessarily invent the phenomenon.) But what do we call it when someone decides to turn tail and leave a situation immediately, without any explanation at all? These days, there doesn’t seem to be a name for a sudden, unexpected exit. Back in the 1800s , however, there was one, courtesy of the third president, Thomas Jefferson .

The phrase: “My name is Haines.”

This may sound a bit strange, but it all stems from an unusual interaction Jefferson had while in office with a member of the opposition party. According to Monticello.org , The Weekly Picayune originally published the story in New Orleans on February 17, 1840.

The story behind “My name is Haines” 

According to the story, around 1805, during his second term as president, Jefferson was riding near Monticello, his Virginia residence, when he struck up a conversation with another man on the road. Amusingly, the man had no idea who he was speaking to, and as a staunch member of the Federalist Party, which opposed Jefferson’s Democratic-Republican Party, he had plenty of harsh words for the president.

Thomas Jefferson’s Monticello. Photo credit: Martin Falbisoner/Wikimedia Commons 

The Weekly Picayune wrote:

“Haines took particular pains to abuse Mr. Jefferson; called him all kinds of hard names, ran down every measure of his administration, poked the non-intercourse and embargo acts at him as most outrageous and ruinous, ridiculed his gun-boat…
items.t: Thomas Jefferson coined a hip and funny phrase for abrupt goodbyes that still holds up today

items.title: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
items.summary:
A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. 

“As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” 

Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) 

The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung 
 Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. 

“Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning,…
items.t: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool

items.title: Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise
items.summary:
P arc des Madelinots, a humble wedge of green space in the Verdun borough of Montreal, is not in the most tranquil of settings. The 6,500-square-foot pocket park sits beside a busy junction and is flanked on two sides by roads often filled with cars. 

For years, locals in the historically working-class neighborhood had to deal with the noise of constant passing vehicle traffic while trying to relax, meet with friends, play with their kids or, indeed, do anything else in this outdoor community space.  

But today, Parc des Madelinots is bathed in a very different kind of sound: the lap of ocean waves, dulcet bird calls and the crunch of sand underfoot. 

Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape 
 It’s not because a beach has suddenly arrived in Verdun. The sounds are recordings being broadcast in an attempt to reshape urban noise, fighting sound with sound in a constructive way to reduce noise-induced disturbance, reinvigorate the use of the public space and even preserve cultural memory for displaced communities. 

“Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource,” says Catherine Guastavino, a professor at McGill University and principal investigator of Sounds in the City , a research team that is one of the collaborators on Les Madelinéennes , the sonic project in Parc des Madelinots. “We can use sounds to improve people’s experience of places.”
